opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are roughly three families of approaches, and they're complementary rather than competing.

The first is really about data. People underestimate how much of a model's capability comes from the quality and the structure of what it's trained on, not just the quantity. With small models, you can't afford to waste capacity memorizing noisy web text, so carefully curated or synthesized data matters a lot. A lot of our work, for example symbolic knowledge distillation, where we had a large model generate commonsense knowledge that we then filtered with critic models, showed that a much smaller student can match or even outperform its teacher on specific capabilities if the data is good enough. So the student doesn't have to be a pale copy of the teacher; with the right filtering, it can be better in focused ways.

The second family is about algorithms at training and inference time. Distillation is one, but there's also how you do reinforcement learning or preference optimization, and inference-time search, where you let the model think more, sample multiple candidates, verify, and backtrack. Some of our decoding work showed that clever inference-time algorithms can partly make up for a lack of scale. You trade some compute at inference for parameters, which is often a good trade.

The third is about combining small models with other things: tools, retrieval, symbolic reasoning, or other models in a modular system. A small model doesn't need to store all the world's knowledge in its weights if it can look things up or call a calculator or a solver. That's closer to how humans work, too. We don't memorize everything; we know how to find and reason over things.

Underneath all of this, I have a philosophical motivation. I don't think it's healthy for AI to be something only a handful of companies with enormous compute can build. If we can show that small models, with the right data and algorithms, can be really capable, that democratizes AI for academia, smaller organizations, and countries without massive resources. It also pushes us to understand why these models work, rather than just scaling and hoping. Scale has been amazing, but I think we've been a bit lazy scientifically, and the small-model regime forces us to be smarter.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, because I think there's this prevailing assumption in the field that scale is everything, and the only path forward is bigger and bigger models. And I just don't believe that's the full story. I like to think of it as, you know, David versus Goliath. Can a small model actually beat a much larger one? And I think the answer is yes, if you're clever about it.

So broadly, there are a few different approaches, and I think of them in terms of where the knowledge or the capability is coming from. One is distillation, and this is where a lot of our work has been. The idea is that you use a large model as a teacher, but not in the naive way of just copying its outputs. In our work on symbolic knowledge distillation, for example, we generate data from a large model, and then we filter it very aggressively with a critic model. And what's interesting is that the resulting dataset can actually be higher quality than what humans wrote, and the student model trained on it can outperform the teacher on the specific task. So the student is not just a compressed version of the teacher, it's actually better, because you've concentrated the signal.

The second approach is about inference-time computation. Instead of trying to cram everything into the parameters, you let the small model think harder when it's actually generating. Decoding-time algorithms, search, verifiers, things like that. Our work on NeuroLogic decoding or on using reward models to guide generation falls in this bucket. And this is appealing because a small model with a smart inference procedure can sometimes match a much larger model doing greedy decoding.

And then the third is really about the data itself. I think we've been undervaluing the quality of the training data relative to quantity. If you're careful about what you train on, especially for reasoning, you can get surprisingly far with a small model. We saw this with our work on commonsense, where a carefully curated resource makes a huge difference.

Now, I want to be honest that none of these is a silver bullet. Distillation inherits the teacher's biases, inference-time methods cost latency, and good data is hard to get at scale. But I think the combination is where it gets exciting. And philosophically, I care about this not just for efficiency reasons, but because if the only way to do frontier AI is with enormous compute, then only a handful of organizations get to participate. Small models are a way to keep the research ecosystem diverse and open, and I think that matters for the field as a whole.

astra-6.text:
I think there are several different directions, and they’re complementary. One is to ask, how much can we improve the data that a smaller model learns from? Another is to improve the learning algorithm itself. And then there’s the question of what we ask the model to do on its own, versus giving it access to tools or other sources of knowledge.

The data question is especially interesting to me. With a large model, we tend to throw an enormous amount of text at it and hope that useful capabilities emerge. But a smaller model has less capacity, so the choice of what to teach it becomes really important. Can we give it more informative examples? Can we organize the knowledge in a way that makes the underlying reasoning easier to learn?

One way to do that is to use a larger model to generate training material for a smaller one. But simply imitating the larger model’s answers isn’t necessarily enough. You want to select and verify that material, and you want examples that help the smaller model generalize rather than memorize.

So I wouldn’t frame this as finding one trick that makes a small model equivalent to a large one. It’s about understanding which capabilities actually require scale, and which ones we can achieve through better teaching. I think there’s a lot of room to improve that teaching.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are several different levers, and it’s useful to separate them. One is improving the training data. A small model has limited capacity, so we should be thoughtful about what we ask it to learn. Instead of simply giving it more text, can we give it better examples, better explanations, and a more coherent progression of concepts?

Another is distillation, where a larger model helps train a smaller one. But I think the interesting question is what we transfer. If we only transfer the final answer, we may miss the reasoning or the knowledge that makes that answer possible. At the same time, explanations generated by a larger model can be wrong, so quality control matters.

Then there’s the system around the model: retrieval, tools, and more computation at inference time. A small model doesn’t necessarily need to memorize everything if it can find relevant information and use it effectively.

So I wouldn’t view these as competing approaches. The exciting question is how much capability we can get by combining better data, better learning methods, and better ways of using the model.
